stories.title: Cascadia, 1700
stories.text: The catalog gives it one nominal point off the coast, 45° N 125° W, magnitude 9.0 (mw), with no depth. USGS on the Japanese records of its tsunami: “Some noted that no parent earthquake had been felt; they were wondering what had set off the waves. They had no way knowing that the tsunami had been spawned during an earthquake along the coast of northwestern North America.”

stories.title: New Madrid, 1811–12
stories.text: The catalog lists 4 earthquakes of magnitude 7 or more between 35 and 37.8° N, 91.2 and 88.3° W, from 1811-12-16 to 1812-02-07: 7.5, 7.0, 7.3 and 7.5 (mw), none with a depth. USGS: “They were by far the largest east of the Rocky Mountains in the U.S. and Canada.”

stories.title: San Francisco, 1906
stories.text: Magnitude 7.9 (mw) at 13:12 UTC on 1906-04-18, 11.7 km deep at 37.75° N 122.55° W. One dot for a rupture whose length USGS gives as “The total length is 296 miles (477 kilometers).” In 1906 the catalog lists 6 earthquakes of magnitude 2.5 or more between 32.4 and 42.1° N, 124.5 and 114° W.

stories.title: Alaska, 1964
stories.text: Magnitude 9.2 (mw) at 03:36 UTC on 1964-03-28, 25 km deep; the catalog still lists this solution as automatic. USGS: it “is the most powerful recorded earthquake in U.S. history.” In 1964 the Alaska map box holds 147 earthquakes of magnitude 4 or more, 143 of them from that day on.

stories.title: Oklahoma, 2009–2017
stories.text: Magnitude 3 and up between 33.6 and 37° N, 103 and 94.4° W: 4 in 2008, 888 in 2015, 6 in 2025. The largest was magnitude 5.8 (mww) on 2016-09-03, 14 km NW of Pawnee, Oklahoma. USGS: “The majority of earthquakes in Oklahoma are caused by the industrial practice known as "wastewater disposal".”

stories.title: Kīlauea, 2018
stories.text: From 2018-04-30 to 2018-08-31 the catalog lists 12 565 earthquakes of magnitude 2.5 or more on and around the Island of Hawaii. The largest, magnitude 6.9 (mw) on 2018-05-04, was 5.8 km deep. USGS: “In 2018, Kīlauea Volcano experienced its largest lower East Rift Zone (LERZ) eruption and caldera collapse in at least 200 years.”

stories.title: Ridgecrest, 2019
stories.text: Magnitude 6.4 (mw) at 17:33 UTC on 2019-07-04, then magnitude 7.1 (mw) at 03:19 UTC on 2019-07-06, 33.8 hours later and 8 km deep. USGS: “another stronger earthquake shook the area about 33 hours later.” In July 2019 the catalog lists 2 516 earthquakes of magnitude 2.5 or more between 32.4 and 42.1° N, 124.5 and 114° W.

sources.quote: Beginning in 2009, Oklahoma experienced a surge in seismicity. This surge was so large that its rate of magnitude 3 and larger earthquakes exceeded California's from 2014 through 2017.
